_note: Radiology reading-room cases. Synthetic Indian vignettes paired with openly licensed images (Wikimedia Commons). Read by src/data/radiology.ts and backend/radiology.py. Keywords are lower-case phrases for the offline grader.

cases.vignette: Pre-employment health check for a nursing job in Bengaluru. No cough, fever or breathlessness. Never smoked. No TB contact. Examination normal, SpO2 99% on air.

findings.label: Adequate PA film: not rotated, good inspiration, well penetrated
findings.probe: Before the pathology, is this film technically adequate? How would you check?

findings.label: Trachea central, mediastinum not shifted
findings.probe: Where is the trachea?

findings.label: Both lung fields clear, no consolidation, mass or nodules
findings.probe: Go through the lungs zone by zone. Anything in either lung?

findings.label: Costophrenic angles sharp, no effusion
findings.probe: What about the costophrenic angles?

findings.label: Heart size normal (cardiothoracic ratio under 0.5)
findings.probe: Is the heart a normal size? How do you measure it?

findings.label: Diaphragms normal, no free gas; bones and soft tissues intact
findings.probe: Have you looked at the diaphragms and the bones?

teaching: Calling a film normal is a finding too: say it only after you have been through every area in order.
Review areas where lesions hide: apices, behind the heart, below the diaphragm, hila.
Cardiothoracic ratio is only valid on a PA film; an AP film magnifies the heart.

cases.vignette: Four days of high fever with chills, cough with rusty sputum and right-sided chest pain on breathing. RR 26/min, SpO2 91% on air, BP 110/70. Bronchial breath sounds over the right lower front of the chest.

findings.label: Homogeneous airspace opacity (consolidation) in the right mid to lower zone
findings.probe: Compare the two lungs zone by zone. Is one side whiter than the other?

findings.label: Right heart border obscured (silhouette sign), localising it to the right middle lobe
keywords: loss of the right heart border
findings.probe: Can you see the right heart border clearly? What does that tell you?

findings.label: Air bronchograms within the opacity
findings.probe: Inside that white area, do you see any dark branching lines?

findings.label: Trachea central, no volume loss (so consolidation, not collapse)
findings.probe: Is there any volume loss? How would you tell consolidation from collapse?

findings.label: Costophrenic angles clear, no significant effusion
findings.probe: Any fluid at the bases?

findings.label: Left lung clear
findings.probe: And the left lung?

distractors: Right middle lobe collapse from an endobronchial tumour
teaching: Silhouette sign: an opacity touching the right heart border lies in the middle lobe; one that blurs the hemidiaphragm lies in the lower lobe.
Consolidation keeps lung volume (trachea central); collapse pulls the trachea and fissures toward it.
Score CURB-65 at the bedside; this man is 67 with RR 26, so think about admission.
Repeat the film at about 6 weeks in older smokers to make sure it clears and nothing was hiding behind it.

credit.author: Bonilla A, Blair AJ, Alamro SM, et al., J Med Case Reports 2019

cases.vignette: Tall, thin engineering student who smokes. Sudden sharp right-sided chest pain and breathlessness while sitting in class two hours ago. HR 98, BP 124/78, SpO2 95%. Reduced breath sounds and hyper-resonance on the right.

findings.label: Visible visceral pleural line on the right (arrows)
findings.probe: Look carefully at the right upper and lateral chest. Can you see a fine white line?

findings.label: No lung markings lateral to the pleural line on the right
findings.probe: What do you see beyond that line, out toward the chest wall?

findings.label: Right side involved, partially collapsed right lung
findings.probe: Which side is it, and how much lung has collapsed?

findings.label: No mediastinal shift, so no radiological tension
findings.probe: Is there anything here that makes this an emergency right now? Where is the mediastinum?

findings.label: Size estimate: rim of air under 2 cm at the hilum level (small)
findings.probe: How would you size it, and why does the size matter?

teaching: Look for the thin white visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it; arrows here help, a real film will not.
Tension is a clinical diagnosis (hypotension, hypoxia, shift); never wait for a film to decompress it.
BTS: a primary spontaneous pneumothorax that is small and not breathless can be observed; larger or symptomatic ones need aspiration or a small drain.
Advise him to stop smoking and avoid flying until resolved; he must never scuba dive without definitive surgery.

cases.study: Chest X-ray, PA view (film on a light box)
cases.vignette: Chronic kidney disease on irregular dialysis. Two weeks of worsening breathlessness, can only sleep propped up, swollen legs. RR 28, SpO2 89% on air. Stony dull percussion and absent breath sounds over both lower chests.

findings.label: Dense homogeneous opacity in both lower zones
findings.probe: Compare the lower halves of both lungs. What do you see?

findings.label: Both costophrenic angles obliterated
findings.probe: Can you see the costophrenic angles?

findings.label: Meniscus sign: concave upper border rising toward the lateral chest wall
findings.probe: Look at the shape of the upper edge of that white area. What shape is it?

findings.label: Hemidiaphragms and lower heart borders not visible
findings.probe: Can you see the diaphragms?

findings.label: Effusions are bilateral, which points to a systemic cause (fluid overload, heart failure)
findings.probe: Is it one side or both, and what does that suggest about the cause?

teaching: About 200 mL blunts the angle on a PA film; a lateral decubitus film or ultrasound picks up much less.
Bilateral effusions are usually transudates (fluid overload, heart failure, low albumin); a one-sided exudate in India is TB until proven otherwise.
Tap the fluid if the cause is unclear and use Light's criteria; do the tap under ultrasound.
For her, the treatment is dialysis and fluid removal, not a chest drain.

cases.vignette: Long-standing hypertension, poorly controlled. Three months of breathlessness on climbing stairs and ankle swelling. Displaced, heaving apex beat in the 6th intercostal space. BP 170/100.

findings.label: PA film, so the heart size can be judged
findings.probe: Can you comment on heart size on any film? What projection is this?

findings.label: Cardiothoracic ratio more than 0.5
findings.probe: How big is the heart compared with the chest? Give me a number.

findings.label: Enlarged cardiac silhouette with the apex displaced to the left and down
findings.probe: Describe the shape of the heart shadow. Where is the apex?

findings.label: Look for failure: upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, effusions (lungs here largely clear)
findings.probe: With a big heart, what else would you look for in the lungs?

findings.label: Costophrenic angles visible
findings.probe: Any fluid at the bases?

teaching: CTR = widest heart diameter divided by widest inner chest diameter; over 0.5 on a PA film is cardiomegaly.
A big heart on X-ray needs an echo: it tells you which chamber, the ejection fraction and the valves.
A globular 'water bottle' heart with clear lungs makes you think of pericardial effusion instead.
Control his BP and start heart-failure therapy once the echo confirms LV dysfunction.

cases.vignette: Construction worker. Two months of cough, two episodes of blood-streaked sputum, evening fevers, night sweats and 7 kg weight loss. Brother was treated for TB last year. Thin, febrile, crackles over the right upper chest.

findings.label: Patchy infiltrates in the right upper zone (arrowheads)
findings.probe: Which zones are involved? Start at the apices.

findings.label: Cavity: a thick-walled lucency within the right upper zone opacity
findings.probe: Inside the right upper zone, is there a dark area surrounded by white? What do you call that?

findings.label: Bilateral disease: infiltrates in the left upper and mid zone too
findings.probe: Is the other lung completely clear?

findings.label: Upper zone predominance, typical of post-primary TB
findings.probe: Which part of the lungs is this disease favouring, and why does that matter?

teaching: Upper zone infiltrates with a cavity in a patient with weight loss and haemoptysis is TB until proven otherwise.
Send two sputum samples for CBNAAT or Truenat (rifampicin resistance in one go) under NTEP and notify on Ni-kshay.
Cavitary disease is highly infectious: mask the patient, ventilate the room, and screen household contacts.
Abscesses usually have an air-fluid level and a lower-lobe, aspiration pattern; cancer cavities are thick and irregular.

cases.vignette: Hysterectomy 8 years ago. Two days of colicky central abdominal pain, repeated bilious vomiting, distension, and no flatus since yesterday. Tinkling bowel sounds. Hernial orifices empty.

findings.label: Dilated small bowel loops (over 3 cm) in the central abdomen
findings.probe: Which bowel is dilated, small or large? How do you tell?

findings.label: Multiple air-fluid levels at different heights (step-ladder) on the erect film
findings.probe: This is an erect film. What do you see inside those loops?

findings.label: Valvulae conniventes crossing the full width of the bowel
findings.probe: What do the mucosal folds look like?

findings.label: Little or no gas in the colon and rectum
findings.probe: Is there any gas in the large bowel or rectum?

findings.label: No free gas
findings.probe: What must you always exclude on an acute abdomen film?

teaching: 3-6-9 rule: small bowel over 3 cm, colon over 6 cm, caecum over 9 cm is dilated.
Previous surgery means adhesions; in India also think of obstructed hernia and abdominal TB.
Drip and suck: NG tube, IV fluids, correct potassium, catheter and charting; CT abdomen shows the transition point.
Peritonism, fever, raised lactate or constant pain suggests strangulation and needs urgent surgery.

cases.study: Chest X-ray, supine (resus bay) for an acute abdomen

cases.vignette: Takes diclofenac most days for back pain, smokes. Sudden severe upper abdominal pain 6 hours ago, now everywhere. Lying still, board-like rigid abdomen, absent bowel sounds. HR 118, BP 100/64.

findings.label: Free gas under the left hemidiaphragm
findings.probe: Look just under the diaphragm on each side. Is there anything there that should not be?

findings.label: Diaphragm seen as a thin line with gas above and below it
findings.probe: How can you be sure that gas is outside the stomach?

findings.label: Distinguished from the gastric fundus bubble (no rugae, no fluid level, crescent shape)
findings.probe: On the left, what normal structure contains gas under the diaphragm? How is this different?

findings.label: Supine film: free gas is harder to see; an erect film or CT is more sensitive
findings.probe: What projection is this, and how does that affect seeing free gas?

findings.label: Lungs clear, lines and ECG leads in place
findings.probe: Anything else on the chest itself?

cases.diagnosis: Pneumoperitoneum from a perforated peptic ulcer
teaching: An erect chest film after sitting up for 10 minutes shows as little as 1 to 2 mL of free gas; CT is more sensitive still.
NSAIDs plus smoking plus sudden pain and a rigid abdomen is a perforated ulcer until proven otherwise.
Resuscitate, nil by mouth, NG tube, IV PPI and antibiotics, and call the surgeons now: this needs a laparotomy or laparoscopic repair.
Chilaiditi sign is bowel between liver and diaphragm: you see haustra or folds, and the patient is not sick.

cases.vignette: Diabetic smoker. One hour of crushing central chest pain radiating to the left arm, sweating and vomiting. HR 110, BP 140/90, SpO2 95%. ECG done in triage.

findings.label: Sinus tachycardia, about 110 per minute
findings.probe: Start with the rate and rhythm.

findings.label: ST elevation in V2 to V5 (anterior)
keywords: st elevation in the anterior leads
st elevation in the chest leads
findings.probe: Look at the chest leads. What is happening to the ST segments, and in which leads?

findings.label: ST elevation also in I and aVL (high lateral extension)
findings.probe: Does it extend beyond the chest leads? Check the limb leads.

findings.label: Reciprocal ST depression in the inferior leads (III, aVF)
findings.probe: When you see ST elevation, what do you look for in the opposite leads?

findings.label: Territory: anterior wall, LAD artery
findings.probe: Which artery is blocked?

teaching: STEMI: new ST elevation in two contiguous leads (at least 2 mm in V2 to V3 in men, 1 mm elsewhere) with symptoms.
Reciprocal depression makes infarction far more likely than pericarditis, which gives widespread concave ST elevation and PR depression.
Time is muscle: primary PCI within 90 minutes if available, otherwise thrombolysis (tenecteplase or streptokinase) within 30 minutes of arrival.
Give aspirin 300 mg, a second antiplatelet and heparin per protocol; check for contraindications to lysis.

cases.vignette: Hypertensive and diabetic. Three days of fluttering in the chest and tiredness. Pulse irregularly irregular, apex rate about 100. BP 150/86. No chest pain.

findings.label: Irregularly irregular rhythm (R-R intervals vary with no pattern)
findings.probe: Take a piece of paper along the rhythm strip. Are the R waves evenly spaced?

findings.label: No P waves; fibrillatory (f) baseline
findings.probe: Before each QRS, is there a P wave?

findings.label: Narrow QRS complexes
findings.probe: How wide are the QRS complexes?

findings.label: Ventricular rate about 100 (controlled to borderline)
findings.probe: What is the ventricular rate? How do you count it when the rhythm is irregular?

cases.diagnosis: Atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response
teaching: Irregularly irregular plus no P waves equals AF. With an irregular rhythm count the QRS complexes in 10 seconds and multiply by 6.
Score CHA2DS2-VASc (she scores at least 5) and HAS-BLED; she needs anticoagulation unless contraindicated.
Rate control first in the elderly (beta-blocker or diltiazem; digoxin if sedentary or in heart failure).
In a young Indian patient with AF, listen for a mid-diastolic murmur: rheumatic mitral stenosis is still common.

cases.study: Rhythm strips, two leads recorded together
cases.vignette: Two blackouts this week without warning, one while sitting at breakfast. Dizzy now. HR 38 and regular, BP 100/60. Intermittent cannon a waves in the JVP. Not on any rate-slowing drugs.

findings.label: Slow regular ventricular rate (bradycardia, about 40)
findings.probe: What is the ventricular rate?

findings.label: P waves regular and faster than the QRS rate (more P waves than QRS)
findings.probe: Now forget the QRS. Find every P wave. Are they regular? How many are there?

findings.label: No relationship between P waves and QRS complexes (AV dissociation, PR varies)
findings.probe: Does the PR interval stay the same from beat to beat?

findings.label: QRS is an escape rhythm (note its width: wide means a ventricular escape)
findings.probe: Where are those QRS complexes coming from?

distractors: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block
teaching: In complete heart block P waves march through at their own rate and the QRS follows its own slower escape rate.
Mobitz II: constant PR with sudden dropped beats. CHB: the PR keeps changing because there is no conduction at all.
Syncope with CHB (Stokes-Adams) needs a permanent pacemaker; meanwhile atropine, then transcutaneous pacing or isoprenaline if unstable.
Look for reversible causes: inferior MI, hyperkalaemia, digoxin, beta-blockers, Lyme disease.

credit.author: Dr. Michael-Joseph F. Agbayani and Dr. Eddieson Gonzales

cases.vignette: Chronic kidney disease stage 5, missed her last two dialysis sessions because of travel. Generalised weakness and tingling. HR 80, BP 150/90. Labs pending.

findings.label: Tall, narrow, peaked (tented) T waves, most obvious in the chest leads
findings.probe: Look at the T waves. Are they the shape and height you expect?

findings.label: Small or flattened P waves
findings.probe: Now the P waves. What has happened to them?

findings.label: Comment on QRS width (widening is a late, dangerous sign)
findings.probe: How wide is the QRS, and why does that matter here?

findings.label: Link to the patient: CKD with missed dialysis means hyperkalaemia until proven otherwise
findings.probe: Put this ECG together with her history. What do you suspect?

distractors: Hyperacute T waves of an early STEMI
teaching: Hyperkalaemia sequence: peaked T, then flat P and long PR, then wide QRS, then sine wave and arrest.
ECG changes mean treat now: 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV to stabilise the heart, then insulin with dextrose and salbutamol to shift potassium.
Remove potassium definitively: dialysis for her; stop ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium-sparing drugs.
Hyperacute T waves of STEMI are broad-based and come with ST change in a territory; hyperkalaemic T waves are narrow and tented.

cases.vignette: Fell from a motorbike without a helmet, hit the left side of his head. Knocked out briefly, then talking normally for an hour, now drowsy and vomiting. GCS 11, left pupil sluggish.

findings.label: Biconvex (lentiform) hyperdense extra-axial collection
findings.probe: Describe the shape of that bright collection. Which way do its borders bulge?

findings.label: On the patient's left (right side of the image)
findings.probe: Which side of the patient is it on? Remember how CT images are displayed.

findings.label: Associated skull fracture
findings.probe: Have you looked at the bone next to the collection?

findings.label: Mass effect: effaced sulci and compression of the adjacent brain
findings.probe: What is the collection doing to the brain beside it?

findings.label: Some bleeding on the opposite side too (contrecoup)
findings.probe: Is that the only abnormality? Look at the other side.

teaching: Extradural blood is biconvex and stops at the sutures because the dura is stuck there; subdural blood is crescentic and crosses sutures.
Classically from a temporal bone fracture tearing the middle meningeal artery; the lucid interval is a trap.
Falling GCS with a dilating pupil is a neurosurgical emergency: protect the airway, call neurosurgery, mannitol or hypertonic saline as a bridge.
Read every CT head with Blood Can Be Very Bad: blood, cisterns, brain, ventricles, bone.

cases.vignette: Takes warfarin for a mechanical valve and drinks heavily. Slipped in the bathroom last night and hit his head. Since morning, confused and weak on one side. GCS 13. INR 3.8.

findings.label: Crescent-shaped hyperdense collection along the cerebral convexity
findings.probe: Describe the shape of that collection against the skull.

findings.label: Crosses suture lines and spreads widely over the hemisphere
findings.probe: Does it stop anywhere, or does it spread over the whole hemisphere?

findings.label: Midline shift away from the collection
findings.probe: Where is the midline?

findings.label: Effaced sulci and a compressed lateral ventricle on the same side
findings.probe: Look at the ventricles and the sulci on that side.

findings.label: Hyperdense (bright) blood, so acute
findings.probe: How old is this blood, judging by its density?

teaching: Subdural bleeds come from torn bridging veins; the elderly, alcohol users and anticoagulated patients are at risk after minor falls.
Acute blood is bright; it becomes grey (isodense) at 1 to 3 weeks and dark when chronic.
Reverse his warfarin now (vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate or FFP) and discuss with neurosurgery.
Thickness over 10 mm or midline shift over 5 mm usually means evacuation.

cases.vignette: Hypertensive diabetic. Woke up yesterday unable to move his right arm and leg and unable to speak. Brought in now, about 30 hours later. Drowsy, right hemiplegia, global aphasia.

findings.label: Large hypodense (dark) area in the left MCA territory involving grey and white matter
findings.probe: Compare the two hemispheres. Is one darker?

findings.label: Left hemisphere (right side of the image), fitting his right-sided weakness and aphasia
findings.probe: Which hemisphere, and does it fit his signs?

findings.label: Loss of grey-white matter differentiation
findings.probe: In that area, can you still tell grey matter from white matter?

findings.label: Mass effect from oedema: midline shift to the right, compressed left lateral ventricle
findings.probe: What is the swelling doing to the midline and the ventricles?

findings.label: No haemorrhage (no hyperdense blood)
findings.probe: Before calling it ischaemic, what must you exclude?

cases.diagnosis: Established left MCA territory ischaemic infarct with cerebral oedema
teaching: Early ischaemia is subtle; a clearly dark, swollen territory like this means the infarct is hours to days old.
He is far outside the thrombolysis window (4.5 hours) and wake-up timing is unknown; thrombectomy decisions need perfusion imaging.
Large MCA infarcts swell at 2 to 5 days: watch GCS, and in younger patients consider decompressive hemicraniectomy.
Aspirin after haemorrhage is excluded, swallow screen before oral intake, and treat BP, sugar and lipids for secondary prevention.

cases.vignette: Mother of four, overweight. Constant right upper abdominal pain for 2 days after a heavy oily meal, radiating to the right shoulder, with fever and vomiting. Temp 38.4, Murphy sign positive. No jaundice.

findings.label: Echogenic (bright) focus in the gallbladder neck
findings.probe: Inside the gallbladder, what do you see?

findings.label: Posterior acoustic shadowing behind it
findings.probe: What happens to the image behind that bright spot?

findings.label: Stone impacted in the neck (does not move with position)
findings.probe: Where exactly is the stone, and does that matter?

findings.label: Thickened gallbladder wall (over 3 mm)
findings.probe: Measure the wall. Is it normal?

findings.label: Correlate with a sonographic Murphy sign and look for pericholecystic fluid and CBD size
findings.probe: What would you check while scanning her, beyond the picture itself?

teaching: A stone is bright, casts a clean acoustic shadow and moves with position; a polyp does not shadow or move.
Stone plus wall over 3 mm plus sonographic Murphy plus fever is acute cholecystitis (Tokyo guidelines).
Treat with fluids, analgesia and antibiotics; early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within a week is best.
In the Gangetic belt gallbladder cancer is common: an irregular wall or mass with stones needs further imaging.

cases.vignette: Post-menopausal, slipped at the vegetable market and fell on her outstretched left hand. Painful, swollen wrist with a dinner-fork deformity. Fingers pink, sensation intact.

findings.label: Transverse fracture of the distal radius metaphysis, about 2 cm above the wrist joint
findings.probe: Trace the cortex of each bone. Where is the break?

findings.label: Dorsal displacement and dorsal angulation of the distal fragment on the lateral view
findings.probe: On the side view, which way has the distal fragment moved?

findings.label: Associated ulnar styloid fracture
findings.probe: Is the radius the only bone broken?

findings.label: Radial shortening / impaction
findings.probe: Compare the lengths of the radius and the ulna at the wrist.

findings.label: Two views at right angles reviewed
findings.probe: How many views do you need for a fracture, and have you used both?

cases.diagnosis: Colles fracture of the left distal radius with ulnar styloid fracture
teaching: Colles: distal radius, dorsal displacement and angulation, from a fall on the outstretched hand. Smith is the reverse (volar).
Check the median nerve and circulation before and after reduction.
Closed reduction under haematoma block and a below-elbow cast, then a check film; unstable or intra-articular fractures need fixation.
A fragility fracture at 64 means osteoporosis: arrange a DEXA scan and start bone protection.

cases.vignette: Slipped on a wet bathroom floor. Cannot stand. The leg is shortened and externally rotated; pain on any hip movement. On treatment for BP; walks with a stick.

findings.label: Fracture line through the femoral neck
findings.probe: Follow the cortex from the femoral head down the neck. Where does it break?

findings.label: Displacement with shortening of the femoral neck
findings.probe: Is the fracture displaced?

findings.label: Shenton's line disrupted
findings.probe: Trace the curve from the inferior border of the femoral neck to the pubic ramus. Is it smooth?

findings.label: Intracapsular (proximal to the trochanters), which risks the femoral head blood supply
findings.probe: Is this inside or outside the joint capsule, and why does that change the operation?

findings.label: Check the pubic rami and the other hip
findings.probe: What else on a pelvis film can mimic a hip fracture?

cases.diagnosis: Displaced intracapsular fracture of the neck of femur
teaching: Shortened, externally rotated leg after a fall in an elderly person is a hip fracture until proven otherwise.
Displaced intracapsular fractures cut off the femoral head blood supply: hemi- or total hip arthroplasty, not fixation, in the elderly.
Extracapsular (intertrochanteric) fractures heal well with a dynamic hip screw or nail.
Operate within 36 hours, give a fascia iliaca block for pain, and screen for delirium, falls risk and osteoporosis.
